prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and bioactive form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 remains the one shortlisted achievement with a complete and independently confirmed arc from physiology (the incretin effect, proglucagon processing, the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its insulinotropic action in humans, receptor biology) to a drug class with large randomized-trial benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Round 1 tested rather than assumed this: no member disputed originality or maturity, and the only live question is the third name. I hold Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Holst and Drucker are the uncontested core. For the third seat I apply one principle: a prize for discovery honours the steps that defined the biological target and made the pharmacology conceivable, and identification and synthesis of the active peptide is such a step, whereas the long-acting analogue is development against an already defined target. The citation wording on enabling therapies is how the prize acknowledges the drug story without a fourth name. I keep this as a single-part prize: a second part would add an attribution burden that none of the alternatives clearly repays.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakness. Habener's group is outside the supplied credit list and the priority record for the active peptide is contested, and I cannot verify it from the files I may use, so a trio with Mojsov rests on a judgment about priority that I have not been able to confirm. Choosing Mojsov over Knudsen can be read as passing over the person whose analogue reached patients, and a discovery-only trio risks looking detached from the medicine that gave the field its prominence. Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating, as the chair notes, though I do not think this bears on the discovery itself. If the Mojsov priority record proves unclear, Knudsen is the safer third name and I would move.

responses.point: Keeps Holst, Drucker and Knudsen with a citation that includes development of long-acting therapies, and argues that including Mojsov without Habener leaves a gap in the record.
responses.response: The Habener point is fair and I count it against my own trio, but it applies to any name drawn from the active-peptide work and does not by itself favour Knudsen. If the priority record is unclear, the problem is a gap in what we can verify, and replacing Mojsov with Knudsen resolves it only by changing the criterion from discovery to development. I accept that the therapy is why GLP-1 ranks first, but that is a reason for the citation to mention therapies, which mine does. I would not oppose your trio as a majority outcome, and I note that you would not oppose B010 as a second part. I still prefer one part because B010 would add its own Medicine-link question without making the GLP-1 allocation easier.

responses.point: Asks the committee to examine the evidence on Mojsov's priority more carefully, and says Knudsen is the safer third name if that record is unclear.
responses.response: I accept your conditional and adopt it as my own test. From the evidence I may use, Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a discovery step and her claim is at least as well grounded as the alternatives for the third seat, but I have not verified the priority history and I will not pretend otherwise. My position is that unresolved dispute should not by itself displace a discovery contribution with an industrial one, so I keep Mojsov. If a colleague can bring evidence that her priority is genuinely unsettled, I would reconsider. Your safety and durability reservation is noted, but chronic-use data concern the drugs and not the discovery being honoured.

responses.point: Now prefers Mojsov to Knudsen as a close call on a discovery-first reading, while warning that the omission of Habener and Knudsen is a real cost the citation should not hide, and ranks optogenetics below CAR-T and the unfolded protein response.
responses.response: We have both moved from Knudsen to Mojsov on the same principle, which answers the chair's question about Linnarsson's configuration. I agree the citation should not hide the cost: my wording says the discoveries enabled incretin-based therapies, which acknowledges the drug story, but I accept that it does not remedy the exclusion of Knudsen or Habener and I would not claim it does. On optogenetics I agree that the channelrhodopsin discovery and the neuronal implementation are separate steps and that no three-name selection is defensible, so I do not support B044 as a second part. On CAR-T I remain more positive than Sandberg, though the missing early chimeric-receptor work is a real credit gap.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because each holds a distinct, defensible part of the discovery chain, while conceding that Knudsen's exclusion invites an objection and that UPR is the more compact credit story.
responses.response: I now agree with your trio and your reasoning that each of the three holds a distinct link in the discovery chain. I do not fully accept your description of Knudsen's contribution as practical engineering, since a durable once-weekly peptide required real insight into binding and half-life, but that is development for a defined target, and that distinction is what decides the third seat. On TOR, I accept your point that Hall and Schreiber without Sabatini leave the mammalian identification out. That is why I have moved TOR out of my alternatives and listed CAR-T instead, where the three credited names are at least internally consistent even though the early chimeric-receptor work is not.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide holds up against the Habener-lab contribution; this cannot be settled from the files I may use, and if it proves unclear I would move to Knudsen.
Whether a majority prefers a physiology-based trio or a physiology-to-therapy trio, which also determines the citation wording.
Whether a second achievement would improve the configuration; I judge that B010 has the cleanest credit but a weaker present Medicine link, and CAR-T has a credit gap at its origin.
How much weight clinical translation should carry against basic discovery for B010, where therapies are still pending.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field is autoimmunity (Sjogren's disease, lupus, Ro52/TRIM21), adjacent to cGAS-STING (B009) and CAR-T in autoimmunity, which is topical overlap and not a personal or institutional connection. Known co-authors (Vijay Kuchroo, Sven-Erik Sonesson) are not credited on any shortlisted candidate, and my Bergen affiliation and shared KI setting do not establish a tie to any credited person. No update to my round-1 disclosure and no recusal is requested.
